title: Dealing with miscounted stitches
subtitle: Why stitch count drifts, how to find where it went wrong, and when to fix it
excerpt: A stitch count that doesn't match the pattern at the end of a row means a stitch was added or lost somewhere. Most drifting counts come from two places: working into the turning chain as a stitch when it isn't, or missing the first or last stitch of a row.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book — counting and stitch problems. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet.

glossaryTerms.definition: A gradual change in stitch count across multiple rows, where the row edges grow narrower or wider. Caused by consistently adding or losing one stitch per row.

A running count of stitches made by adding a mark (on paper, phone notepad, or using a tally counter) for each completed stitch, used when the stitch count per row is too high to hold in working memory.

heroPrompt: A crochet swatch in cream DK cotton showing clearly narrowing edges after five rows — the stitch drift visible as the piece becomes slightly trapezoid rather than rectangular.

content.text: The most common sign of a miscounted row is

: the edges of the work slowly growing narrower or wider each row. Count the stitches at the end of every row until counting becomes automatic — early detection is much faster to fix than discovering the problem ten rows later.

attrs.heading: Stitch count problems
attrs.intro: The majority of counting errors come from these two places.

items.symptom: Piece narrows row by row (losing stitches)
items.cause: Missing the first stitch of each new row — the stitch directly below the turning chain. The turning chain brings the yarn up but the first actual stitch beside it is being skipped.
items.fix: After turning and chaining, work the first stitch into the stitch immediately beside the turning chain — not into the chain itself (unless the pattern specifies the turning chain counts as a stitch). Lay the work flat and look: the V-shaped top of the first stitch should be clearly visible to the right of the turning chain.

items.symptom: Piece widens row by row (gaining stitches)
items.cause: Working an extra stitch into the turning chain of the previous row. On double crochet patterns where the turning chain does NOT count as a stitch, the chain top looks like a stitch and new crocheters often work into it.
items.fix: Identify the last real stitch of each row by counting back from the edge. The last stitch is the V-top directly beside the turning chain — the chain itself should not receive a stitch. Mark the last stitch with a stitch marker until the habit is established.

content.text: Count by touching each V-top lightly with a finger as you count. Counting by eye across 30+ stitches is unreliable.
: place stitch markers every 10 stitches as you work. Count the groups of 10 at the end of the row rather than counting 200 stitches continuously.
